key_claims: Older American English monolinguals showed delayed MMN responses in the left hemisphere and midline compared to younger monolinguals and bilinguals.
Older Spanish-English bilinguals showed delayed MMN only at a single frontal site compared to younger bilinguals.
Older bilinguals demonstrated relatively preserved MMN responses compared to monolingual peers.
Older bilingual adults showed enlarged N1 amplitudes relative to all other groups.
The findings suggest a dissociation between early sensory encoding and automatic speech discrimination processes.
Lifelong bilingualism may support more adaptable auditory discrimination mechanisms during aging.
limitations: The source does not provide full statistical details or effect sizes.
The sample sizes are relatively small (n=11-14 per group).
The study used unfamiliar Japanese vowel contrasts, which may not generalize to other speech contrasts.
The source does not report on potential confounding variables such as hearing aid use or cognitive status.
what_not_to_say: The study proves that bilingualism prevents age-related auditory decline.
The study shows that bilingualism causes neural resilience or cognitive reserve.
The study provides clinical recommendations for older adults.
The study indicates that older bilinguals have better hearing than monolinguals.
The study demonstrates that bilingualism improves speech perception in all contexts.
